n01.q: A shop's daily sales are a Python list of 500 numbers and the total is needed once per page load. Why convert it to an array, and what is the cost of doing it on every request?
n01.answer: An array makes the total one compiled reduction (`np.array(sales).sum()`) instead of a Python loop, but the conversion itself copies 500 values. Convert once when the data is loaded or cached, not on every request.

followUps.q: What would you measure to decide whether that conversion cost actually matters?
followUps.answer: Time `np.array(sales)` and `.sum()` separately on realistic sizes, and compare against the budget of a page load. If conversion dominates, cache the array instead of benchmarking on 10 values.

followUps.q: Where should the conversion live so every request reuses one array?
followUps.answer: At the data-loading boundary: parse once into an array when the dataset is read or refreshed, keep it alongside the source, and let request handlers read the cached array.

n01.q: Marketing sends 30 marks as strings from a CSV. What breaks if you call np.array on them and then .mean()?
n01.answer: np.array keeps them as a string dtype (or object), so .mean() raises because there is no numeric meaning. Convert with `.astype(float)` (or parse at load time) before any arithmetic.

followUps.q: How do you detect a string dtype before calling `.mean()`?
followUps.answer: `a.dtype.kind` is `U`, `S` or `O` for text-like data, and `.mean()` has no numeric meaning there — convert at load time with an explicit `astype(float)`.

followUps.q: What if only some rows are unparseable?
followUps.answer: Convert strictly so the error surfaces, then validate row by row and report which rows failed; silently replacing bad values with 0 changes the mean.

n02.q: A bug report says an image has shape (0, 256, 3). What does that tell you about the array, and what will happen when you plot it?
n02.answer: The first axis (height) is zero, so the array holds no pixels at all. Plotting or reshaping will fail or render nothing; the bug is upstream where the image was read, not in the plotting call.

followUps.q: Which check in the loader would stop a zero-size image before it reaches the plot?
followUps.answer: Assert every axis is positive (`all(dim > 0 for dim in arr.shape)`) right after reading, and raise with the source path — the failure belongs where the bad data entered.

followUps.q: What does `.size` report for that array?
followUps.answer: Zero, because the product of the axis lengths includes the zero-height axis. A zero size is the fastest way to spot it programmatically.

n02.q: Someone allocates np.empty((1000, 1000)) to save time and sees random huge numbers. Is NumPy broken?
n02.answer: No — empty only allocates the buffer without writing values, so it exposes whatever was in memory. Use np.zeros or np.full when a known starting value is required.

followUps.q: When is `np.empty` actually appropriate?
followUps.answer: When the very next statement writes every element (a preallocated output buffer), so uninitialised garbage can never be read.

followUps.q: Why does NumPy skip zeroing the memory?
followUps.answer: Initialising is a full pass over the buffer; skipping it is a deliberate speed trade for callers who will overwrite the array immediately.

n03.q: A test fixture needs 50 points from 0 to 10 inclusive. Why is np.linspace(0, 10, 50) safer than np.arange(0, 10, 0.2)?
n03.answer: linspace takes a count and always includes both ends; arange takes a step, can include the stop unexpectedly with float steps, and can produce 50 or 51 points depending on rounding. Choose by count when the count is the requirement.

followUps.q: When is `arange` the better call than `linspace`?
followUps.answer: When the step is the requirement — integer ranges and fixed increments where the count is incidental. `linspace` wins when the count is what the test asserts.

followUps.q: How do you confirm the count before relying on it?
followUps.answer: Check `.size` (and the first/last values) on a tiny equivalent range first; float steps are exactly where off-by-one surprises appear.

n03.q: An identity matrix is needed for a 3×4 system, but np.identity(3, 4) raises. What is the right call?
n03.answer: identity only builds square matrices. Use np.eye(3, 4) (rows, columns), which puts ones on the main diagonal of a rectangular shape.

followUps.q: What does the second argument of `np.eye` change?
followUps.answer: The number of columns: `np.eye(3, 4)` is three rows by four columns, with ones on the main diagonal and zeros elsewhere.

followUps.q: How would you build the same rectangular identity without `eye`?
followUps.answer: `a = np.zeros((3, 4)); np.fill_diagonal(a, 1)` — useful when the diagonal value is not 1.

n04.q: A price column is stored as float64 and cast to int to save memory; customers see 99 instead of 99.99. What went wrong?
n04.answer: astype(int) truncates toward zero, it does not round. Either round first (`np.round(price).astype(int)`) or keep cents as integers at the source; casting decimals to integers always loses the fraction.

followUps.q: Which rounding rule does `np.round` use at exactly .5?
followUps.answer: Round-half-to-even (banker's rounding), so 2.5 becomes 2 and 3.5 becomes 4. Code that assumes "always up" is wrong at the boundary.

followUps.q: Why are integer cents often preferred for money?
followUps.answer: Integer arithmetic is exact within range, so sums do not drift; convert to a display string only at the edge.

n04.q: An int32 array of large sensor counters overflows silently negative. How would you have caught it before shipping?
n04.answer: Check np.result_type and the dtype's maximum (np.iinfo(np.int32).max) against the expected range, or promote to int64. NumPy does not raise on overflow for integer arithmetic, so the check has to be explicit.

followUps.q: How do you detect an overflow after it happened?
followUps.answer: Compare the result against `np.iinfo(dtype).min/max`, or watch for a sign flip; a negative counter or wrapped value is the fingerprint of overflow.

followUps.q: Why does NumPy not raise the way Python ints do?
followUps.answer: NumPy uses fixed-width machine integers for speed, so overflow wraps by definition; detecting it costs a check on every operation.

n05.q: A log array has 1000 rows and you need the last 10 rows only. Which expression keeps memory low?
n05.answer: `logs[-10:]` returns a view of the last ten rows without copying the other 990. Copy only if the slice will be mutated after the original is reused.

followUps.q: When is copying that slice the right call?
followUps.answer: When the selection outlives the parent array or will be mutated while the parent is still in use — a copy makes the lifetime independent.

followUps.q: How do you prove a slice did not copy?
followUps.answer: `np.shares_memory(parent, view)` (or `view.base is parent`) answers it directly, without guessing from timings.

n05.q: Why does `matrix[:, 1]` give a different result shape than `matrix[:, 1:2]`, and which one should be used before subtracting a column vector?
n05.answer: `matrix[:, 1]` is 1-D (shape (rows,)) while `matrix[:, 1:2]` is 2-D (shape (rows, 1)). The 2-D form broadcasts correctly against a row; the 1-D form may broadcast along the wrong axis.

followUps.q: What shape does `matrix[:, [1]]` give?
followUps.answer: `(rows, 1)` — a list index keeps the axis, unlike the integer index that drops it.

followUps.q: Which form makes the intent clearest in review?
followUps.answer: The slice form with a short comment, or an explicit `.reshape(-1, 1)` when the reason is broadcasting rather than selection.

n06.q: A rolling window is extracted with `series[i:i+window]` and stored in a list; later someone edits one window and the whole series changes. Why?
n06.answer: Each slice is a view of the same buffer, so editing the window edits the series. Copy the window (`series[i:i+window].copy()`) when it will be stored and modified independently.

followUps.q: What is the cheapest fix if callers expect independent windows?
followUps.answer: Copy at extraction (`series[i:i+window].copy()`); it costs one buffer per window but removes hidden coupling.

followUps.q: How do you test that a helper returns a copy?
followUps.answer: Mutate the returned array and assert the input is unchanged, or assert `np.shares_memory(result, source)` is False.

n06.q: Reversing a 200 MB price series with `[::-1]` takes almost no time. What did NumPy actually do?
n06.answer: It returned a view with negative strides — no data was moved. Any operation that needs contiguous order (such as some libraries' C-API calls) will copy later, which is where the cost appears.

followUps.q: Which later operations force a real copy after a reverse?
followUps.answer: Anything needing contiguous layout: `np.ascontiguousarray`, C-API consumers, and some library calls. The copy happens there, not at the slice.

followUps.q: How do you measure whether the copy happened?
followUps.answer: Check `.flags['C_CONTIGUOUS']` and `np.shares_memory`, or watch resident memory before and after the operation rather than timing the slice alone.

n07.q: A model expects (samples, features) but the loader produced (features, samples). Which fix is safer: reshape, transpose or resize?
n07.answer: Transpose (`.T`) or reshape with explicit dimensions; resize is not a NumPy ndarray method and reshape alone can scramble the value order. Verify with a known 2×3 array before trusting the shape.

followUps.q: How do you verify `reshape` did not scramble values?
followUps.answer: Compare `a.reshape(new).ravel()` with `a.ravel()`; if the value order differs, a copy with the wrong order was used somewhere.

followUps.q: Why can reshape reorder data after a transpose?
followUps.answer: The default `order='C'` re-packs a non-contiguous view into C order, so the logical order changes; pass the order you mean or copy deliberately.

n07.q: Two arrays of shape (100, 3) are joined with np.vstack and the result is (200, 3). Was np.concatenate with axis=0 the same thing here?
n07.answer: Yes — vstack is concatenate along axis 0 after promoting 1-D inputs to rows. The distinction matters for 1-D inputs, where vstack adds a row axis and concatenate does not.

followUps.q: What does `np.concatenate` do with two 1-D arrays on axis=0?
followUps.answer: It joins them end to end, without adding a row axis — the key difference from `vstack`.

followUps.q: Which tool would you use to join by a key instead of position?
followUps.answer: Not a NumPy join: sort both arrays and use `searchsorted`/boolean masks, or let pandas merge by key and convert back to arrays.

n08.q: A revenue calculation is off by 0.01 in the last row. Is the formula wrong?
n08.answer: Almost certainly not — binary floating point cannot represent most decimals exactly, so equality checks and repeated additions drift. Compare with np.isclose and round only for display, not for intermediate maths.

followUps.q: Which tolerance would you choose for money in `np.isclose`?
followUps.answer: For a float display path, `atol` around 1e-9 with the same units; for accounting, store integer cents so the tolerance question disappears.

followUps.q: Why can repeated addition drift more than `np.sum`?
followUps.answer: `np.sum` uses pairwise summation, keeping partial sums similar in magnitude; a naïve loop adds a small number to a large one repeatedly and loses low bits.

n08.q: A running total is needed per row. Which is cheaper: a Python loop with a counter or np.add.accumulate?
n08.answer: accumulate runs one compiled pass and allocates one output array; the loop pays interpreter overhead per element. For very long arrays the difference is orders of magnitude.

followUps.q: What does `accumulate` return compared with `reduce`?
followUps.answer: `accumulate` returns the whole running array, while `reduce` collapses it to the final scalar.

followUps.q: How would you measure the speedup honestly?
followUps.answer: Time both implementations on the same input with `timeit`, several repeats, and report the median — not one lucky run.

n09.q: A store table has shape (500, 1) of discounts and a product table (1, 12) of prices. What happens on addition, and how much memory does the result take?
n09.answer: Both broadcast to (500, 12): every product price meets every store discount. The result is materialised, so it costs 500×12 values even though the inputs are tiny — a real memory risk at scale.

followUps.q: How do you avoid materialising the full (500, 12) product?
followUps.answer: Chunk one axis and reduce as you go (or use `np.einsum` over chunks) when only aggregates are needed; the full product is only worth it when every cell is used.

followUps.q: Does `broadcast_to` itself allocate the big result?
followUps.answer: No — it returns a read-only view with zero strides; the allocation happens on the first arithmetic that materialises values.

n09.q: An operation fails with 'operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (4,) (3, 1)'. What is the actual mismatch?
n09.answer: The trailing dimensions must match or be 1: (4,) is treated as (1, 4), which cannot pair with (3, 1) on the last axis (4 vs 1 is fine, but 1 vs 3 on the first axis gives 4 vs 3 ... ). Fix by reshaping to (4, 1) or (1, 3) so the intended axis pairs.

followUps.q: Which reshape resolves `(4,)` against `(3, 1)`?
followUps.answer: `(3, 1)` wants a length-3 axis matched against something of length 3; reshape the vector to `(1, 3)` for a row pairing or `(4, 1)` for a column pairing, depending on which axis you mean.

followUps.q: How do you read broadcast compatibility quickly?
followUps.answer: Align shapes from the right; each pair must be equal or one of them 1. Incompatible means neither rule holds.

n10.q: A dashboard reports the mean order value as 850, but the median is 120. Which number should be shown to explain 'typical' spending?
n10.answer: The median — a few very large orders pull the mean up. Report both when the distribution is skewed, and say which is which.

followUps.q: Which percentile would you add next to the dashboard?
followUps.answer: p95 (or p99) for the tail: it shows the expensive orders the mean hides, and it needs no assumption about the distribution.

followUps.q: How do you compute a mean that ignores outliers?
followUps.answer: Define the rule first (for example drop values beyond the 1st–99th percentile), mask them, then use `np.mean` — and document the rule next to the number.

n10.q: A (1000, 12) table of monthly sales needs the yearly total per product. Which axis, and what does the result shape look like?
n10.answer: axis=1 collapses the months, giving one value per row (shape (1000,)); axis=0 would give one value per month.

followUps.q: How do you get both row and column totals in one pass?
followUps.answer: `total = table.sum()` plus `axis=1` and `axis=0` reductions, or use `keepdims` so the two can be broadcast against each other.

followUps.q: What does `keepdims` change for later broadcasting?
followUps.answer: It keeps the reduced axis as length 1, so dividing a row by its total aligns automatically instead of failing on shape.

n11.q: Customers with no purchases for 90 days must be flagged. Why is a boolean mask better than a loop that appends indices?
n11.answer: The mask is one vectorised comparison over the whole column, and it can be reused for counting, filtering and assignment. A Python loop grows a list and pays per-row overhead.

followUps.q: How do you reuse one mask for counting and assignment?
followUps.answer: Build it once (`mask = arr > threshold`), then `mask.sum()` for the count and `arr[mask] = value` for the update — same mask, one comparison pass.

followUps.q: What does the mask cost in memory?
followUps.answer: One byte per element (bool), which is why a mask over a huge float64 array is usually affordable.

n11.q: A codebase updates churn labels with `df[mask] = 1` then checks `df` and finds nothing changed. What kind of object was df likely to be?
n11.answer: A NumPy array's boolean assignment does mutate in place, so if nothing changed the value was probably a copy (advanced indexing on a pandas object, or a slice that was copied earlier). Verify with `base is`/`np.shares_memory`.

followUps.q: How do you detect an accidental copy in a chain of operations?
followUps.answer: Check `np.shares_memory` after each step, especially after advanced indexing or a pandas round trip, and look at `.base`.

followUps.q: Which assignment form avoids the chained-index copy trap?
followUps.answer: Assign into the array itself (`arr[mask] = 1`), not into a chained result like `df[mask][col] = 1`.

n12.q: The top 5 products by revenue are needed from 200k rows. Why is np.argpartition usually better than np.argsort here?
n12.answer: argpartition only guarantees that the k smallest/largest are separated, in O(n) expected time, while argsort sorts everything in O(n log n). Sort the 5 selected values afterwards for presentation.

followUps.q: How do you get the top 5 in order after `argpartition`?
followUps.answer: Take the five indices it separated, gather those values, and sort just those five descending — a constant-size sort instead of a full one.

followUps.q: What is the worst case of partition-based selection?
followUps.answer: Quickselect-style algorithms can degrade toward quadratic on adversarial inputs; NumPy uses introselect, which falls back to a safer strategy, but the guarantee is still "not a full sort", not a hard O(n) promise.

n12.q: Two product id arrays are compared to find ids in this month but not last month. Which operation gives that, and does order matter?
n12.answer: np.setdiff1d(this_month, last_month) — it returns sorted unique values in the first array that are absent from the second. The result is sorted, not in input order.

followUps.q: How do you keep input order in a set difference?
followUps.answer: `this_month[np.isin(this_month, last_month, invert=True)]` keeps the original order and duplicates; `setdiff1d` is sorted and unique.

followUps.q: What does `assume_unique` change?
followUps.answer: It lets the routine skip deduplication and sorting, which is faster but wrong if the input actually contains repeats.

n13.q: A function slices an array, modifies the slice and returns it; the caller's original data changes too. Is that a bug?
n13.answer: It is a view, so yes for callers who did not expect mutation. Either copy before modifying or document that the function mutates its input; np.shares_memory is the check that proves which one happened.

followUps.q: Which signature makes mutation explicit to callers?
followUps.answer: Either accept an `out=` parameter or return a copy; documenting "mutates its input" in the name/docstring is the minimum when in-place is the point.

followUps.q: How do you pin aliasing in a unit test?
followUps.answer: Assert `np.shares_memory(input_array, returned)` is False for the copy path and True for the view path, with the same fixture.

n13.q: A 1 GB array is transposed and the memory use doubles. Why, when transposing should be free?
n13.answer: `.T` returns a view with swapped strides, but any later operation that requires C-contiguous layout (a library call, ascontiguousarray, some reductions) materialises a copy, which doubles memory.

followUps.q: How do you check contiguity before a library call?
followUps.answer: `arr.flags['C_CONTIGUOUS']` (and `F_CONTIGUOUS` for Fortran order) tells you whether a copy is about to be forced.

followUps.q: What does `order='F'` change in practice?
followUps.answer: It stores columns contiguously; a transposed array is often already F-contiguous, so requesting F can avoid the copy entirely.

n14.q: An A/B test assigns users with `np.random.rand(n) < 0.5`. Why is that worse than `default_rng(seed).random(n) < 0.5`?
n14.answer: The legacy global RNG shares state across the process and cannot be reproduced independently per experiment. A seeded Generator gives a reproducible stream and avoids interference from other code drawing random numbers.

followUps.q: How do you give each experiment its own reproducible stream?
followUps.answer: Spawn independent generators: `default_rng(SeedSequence(seed).spawn(n))`, so experiments cannot consume each other's draws.

followUps.q: What does reproducibility require beyond the seed?
followUps.answer: The same call order and the same generator method — a seeded stream is only reproducible if the sequence of draws is also fixed.

n14.q: A train/test split keeps 80% for training but the same user appears in both sets. What sampling detail was missed?
n14.answer: Sampling rows with replacement (or sampling rows when the unit is a user) splits a user's records across sets. Sample unique user ids without replacement and then select their rows.

followUps.q: How do you split by user without leakage?
followUps.answer: Split unique user ids first, then select rows whose id is in each split; never split rows when the unit is the user.

followUps.q: What result would reveal the leak?
followUps.answer: Test scores suspiciously close to training scores, or the same id appearing in both sets — check both before trusting the metric.

n15.q: A recommender scores 1000 users × 500 items by `user_vec @ item_matrix.T`. What are the shapes, and roughly how many multiplications?
n15.answer: user_vec is (1000, k), item_matrix is (500, k), so the product is (1000, 500): 500,000 scores and 500,000×k multiplications. That is why k is kept small and why chunking matters at scale.

followUps.q: How do you keep the score matrix from exploding memory?
followUps.answer: Chunk the users and compute scores per batch, aggregate or store only what is needed; the full 1000×500 is small, 1e6×1e4 is not.

followUps.q: Which layout makes the matrix product fastest?
followUps.answer: C-contiguous row-major inputs that match BLAS expectations; transposes that force a copy before the multiply are the usual hidden cost.

n15.q: Someone solves a regression with `inv(X.T @ X) @ X.T @ y` and gets a warning about a singular matrix. What should replace it?
n15.answer: np.linalg.lstsq(X, y) (or solve on the normal equations only when well-conditioned). Inverting a near-singular matrix amplifies numerical error; lstsq is the stable, intended tool.

followUps.q: What else does `lstsq` return besides the solution?
followUps.answer: Residuals, rank and singular values — the rank is exactly what tells you the system was deficient.

followUps.q: When is `solve` preferred over `lstsq`?
followUps.answer: For square, well-conditioned systems: it is faster and exact enough, while `lstsq` is the safe choice for overdetermined or rank-deficient problems.

n16.q: A pipeline writes intermediate arrays as CSV and reads them back; float precision changes. Why is .npy the better intermediate format?
n16.answer: CSV stores decimal text, so floats round-trip through formatting and parsing. .npy stores dtype, shape and raw bytes, so the array comes back exactly.

followUps.q: What does `allow_pickle=False` protect against?
followUps.answer: Loading object arrays from untrusted `.npy`/`.npz` files can execute arbitrary code during unpickling; keeping it False rejects those files.

followUps.q: When is CSV still the right choice?
followUps.answer: When humans or non-NumPy tools must read or edit the file; accept the precision loss and keep `.npy` for the numeric pipeline.

n16.q: A 5 GB feature matrix must be read without loading it all. What does np.memmap buy you, and what does it require?
n16.answer: Memory mapping lets the OS page in the parts of the file you touch, so RAM use stays bounded. It requires the file to exist in the right format/dtype and the access pattern to be reasonably local.

followUps.q: What happens if the memmap file changes underneath a reader?
followUps.answer: Reads can see stale or partially written pages — coordinate writers, or write to a new file and swap the path.

followUps.q: Which access pattern is worst for a memmap?
followUps.answer: Random single-element reads spread across a huge file: each page fault costs far more than the value read.

n17.q: A dataset mixes dates as strings and timestamps as ints. Why is one datetime64 array better than two columns?
n17.answer: datetime64 gives one typed axis with real subtraction (timedelta64), ordering and comparison. Two representations force conversion at every use and invite silent unit mistakes (days vs seconds).

followUps.q: How do you convert integer epochs to `datetime64` correctly?
followUps.answer: State the unit: `epochs.astype('datetime64[s]')`; a wrong unit silently shifts every date instead of raising.

followUps.q: What breaks when units are mixed?
followUps.answer: Comparing day and second units truncates to the coarser unit, so two "different" timestamps can compare equal.

n17.q: A record has an id and a score. When is a structured array the right choice over two parallel arrays?
n17.answer: When rows are always used together — sorting, saving and indexing keep the fields aligned. Two parallel arrays are simpler when the fields are analysed separately and independently.

followUps.q: What does sorting a structured array sort by?
followUps.answer: The fields in declaration order unless you pass `order=[...]`, so field order is part of the record contract.

followUps.q: When do parallel arrays beat a structured array?
followUps.answer: When each column is analysed independently and vectorised as its own array; structured records win when rows travel together.

n18.q: Sensor data has -999 as a missing marker. What breaks if it is left in, and what are the two honest fixes?
n18.answer: The marker drags every mean and histogram toward -999. Either replace it with np.nan and use nan-aware reductions, or mask it with numpy.ma so reductions skip it; both must be visible in the output.

followUps.q: How do you make the replacement auditable?
followUps.answer: Count what you changed (`(a == -999).sum()`) and surface that number in the report; a silent fill is indistinguishable from real data.

followUps.q: Which reductions silently ignore NaN?
followUps.answer: Only the `nan*` family (`nansum`, `nanmean`, `nanmedian`); plain `sum`/`mean` propagate NaN by design.

n18.q: np.nanmean returns a number but np.mean returns nan on the same array. Is nanmean always safe?
n18.answer: nanmean ignores NaN by reducing the effective count, so it is safe only when the missingness is random. If NaNs correlate with the value being measured, the mean is biased and that must be reported.

followUps.q: How do you report how much data was missing?
followUps.answer: Count `np.isnan(a).sum()` and its fraction, and attach it to every statistic derived from that column.

followUps.q: What is the risk of filling NaNs with the mean?
followUps.answer: It shrinks the variance and biases correlations toward zero; the filled value looks like data, so the distortion is invisible later.

n19.q: A loop builds a 10,000-element array with np.append per iteration. Why is it slow, and what is the fix?
n19.answer: np.append copies the whole array every call, so the total work is quadratic. Collect values in a Python list and call np.array once, or preallocate an output array and assign by index.

followUps.q: How do you preallocate when the final length is unknown?
followUps.answer: Collect into a Python list (amortised growth) and convert once, or count first and preallocate; avoid per-iteration `np.append`.

followUps.q: What is the real cost of `np.append` in a loop?
followUps.answer: Every call copies the whole existing array, so total work is quadratic in the number of iterations.

n19.q: A hot path allocates a temporary at every step. When is `out=` the right optimisation and when is it a bug risk?
n19.answer: out= is right when the destination is known and not aliased with the inputs; it avoids allocation churn. It is risky when the output is also an input or a view of one, because partial writes can corrupt the computation.

followUps.q: How do you check aliasing before using `out=`?
followUps.answer: `np.shares_memory(out, a)` and `np.shares_memory(out, b)`; any True means partial writes can corrupt the inputs.

followUps.q: Which kind of code benefits most from `out=`?
followUps.answer: A fixed-size ufunc repeated in a loop where the output buffer can be reused across iterations.

n20.q: An image analysis pipeline stores RGB as (height, width, 3). How do you compute per-channel means in one call?
n20.answer: `img.mean(axis=(0, 1))` collapses height and width, leaving one mean per channel (shape (3,)).

followUps.q: How do you get per-channel standard deviation at the same time?
followUps.answer: `img.std(axis=(0, 1))` — same reduction axes, one more statistic, still a single pass over each channel.

followUps.q: What does `axis=(0, 1)` mean in words?
followUps.answer: Reduce over height and width, leaving the channel axis untouched, so the result has one value per channel.

n20.q: A DataFrame column is converted to an array for arithmetic and back to a Series for the report. Where should the conversion live?
n20.answer: At the boundary of the numerical function: take the array in, return an array, and let the caller wrap it back into a Series with the original index. Converting inside the hot path repeats work and loses index alignment.

followUps.q: How do you keep the index aligned after the array round trip?
followUps.answer: Carry the index alongside the array and reattach it on the way back; converting inside the hot function loses it.

followUps.q: When does `.to_numpy()` return a copy instead of a view?
followUps.answer: When the column has a non-NumPy-compatible dtype, is non-contiguous, or mixed types force an object array — pass `copy=False` only when you know the layout is compatible.
